newsitem.title: USA: Congress on UN debt: good will but few commitments.
newsitem.headline: Congress on UN debt: good will but few commitments.

text.p: Despite praise and good will in Washington, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan faced members of Congress reluctant to pay the huge U.S. debt to the United Nations until the world body institutes radical reforms.

Annan's three-day visit, that ended on Friday, followed at least two years of relentless criticism of the United Nations, its detractors ranging from conservatives saying the world body had too much power to radical militia claiming the U.N. flew secret black helicopters around the United States.
The secretary-general, a 58-year old Ghanaian U.N. official who took office on Jan. 1, has made reform of the world body and securing U.S. funding among his primary goals.
But he has also emphasised that reform does not necessarily mean mass firing of staff and hoarding cash, but setting priorities to make the organisation efficient and relevant.

President Bill Clinton pledged to work with Congress to "pay what we owe." And Newt Gingrich, the speaker of the House of Representatives, said Annan showed a "refreshingly new attitude," adding that he thought "we will be able to work this out."
But disagreements were immediately apparent on:

-- The amount of money owed for back dues and peacekeeping missions. The official U.N. records show $1.3 billion. The Clinton administration says $900 million and some key members of Congress put it at $825 million. The discrepancy arises mainly from U.S. legislation to unilaterally decrease contributions to peacekeeping.

-- The amount the United States would pay in the future, which has to be decided in negotiations with other member states and is based on economic wealth. Currently, dues are assessed at 25 percent but Congress wants 20 percent.

-- The amount of credit the United States should receive from its regular dues for voluntary contributions to the United Nations or its related activities. Such a concept, if adopted, could reduce U.S. dues to zero along with those of other leading industrial states.
Annan, in a speech to the National Press Club, reminded Congress that the United States has a treaty obligation to pay U.N. dues and peacekeeping expenses at the current rate.

"I am always willing to help move such a process but this is a challange for American diplomacy, not the secretary general," he said. "The United States can negotiate a lower rate for itself but it must persuade other member states first."

On credits for related activities he told questioners that governments who undertook voluntary activities to promote their national interests or even for humanitarian reasons could not "pass their bill on to the United Nations" without prior approval.

Sen. Jesse Helms, the Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told Annan on Thursday he would introduce legislation shortly linking payments of the U.S. debt to "benchmarks" on the pace of reform.
In an unusual arrangement, Annan agreed to send his staff to consult with the committee before and after the legislation was drafted.
A U.N. official said Annan was "uncomfortable" with the idea of the United Nations setting "benchmarks" or conditions for paying the debt.

Annan, who was elected after the United States blocked his predecessor Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt from assuming a second term, said he was committed to restructuring the United Nations but reminded his listeners he had a constituency of 184 other states.
Said the official: "He has to appear even-handed. He's walking a fine line here."
Annan intends to draw up a wide-ranging reform plan by July and get approval from the 185-member General Assembly by end of 1997.
Asked by reporters how he justified his intensive visit to Washington, he quipped: "I would devote such attention to any government that pays 25 percent of the budget and owed a billion dollars."
